title: What guests call about at night: 6,796 rental phone calls by hour
summary: 6,796 vacation rental calls by local hour: how many come at night, what they're about, how many go unanswered, and an after-hours plan.
body_markdown:
[All posts](https://prohost.ai/blog)


**Most calls to a vacation rental come during the day. In 6,796 inbound calls to the phone lines of 41 rental businesses, only 1 in 20 came between 10pm and 7am at the property. But the night calls are different. Calls after 6pm are about twice as likely to be about getting into the property, and night calls are more likely to go unanswered. So an after-hours phone plan doesn't need to cover everything. It needs to cover access and a short list of real emergencies.**


## Key takeaways


- **4.9% of inbound calls come at night** (10pm to 7am, the property's local time). **17.3%** come after 6pm.
- **The busiest stretch is noon to 6pm.** About half of all calls land in those six hours.
- **Access problems double after dark.** Door codes, locks, keys and gates come up in **17.8%** of evening calls and **16.5%** of night calls, compared with **8.7%** during the day.
- **Maintenance calls rise too:** from **7.8%** of daytime calls to **11.8%** at night.
- **Night calls go unanswered more often.** **15.8%** of night calls never connected to anyone, compared with **12.5%** during the day.
- **Calls are short.** The median answered call lasted **60 seconds** .

## Where we're coming from


I spent 6 years at Airbnb as a staff data scientist on the hosting team, and we host in Hawaii, the Smokies and Joshua Tree, where we hold a[4.99 rating across thousands of guest stays](https://prohost.ai/about) . The question in this post is one every host asks before handing their phone to someone else for the night: what actually comes in after dark? We looked at every inbound call to rental phone lines on ProhostAI over six months to find out.


> **How we measured it.** Inbound calls to ProhostAI phone lines from May 23 to November 18, 2026: 6,796 calls to 41 rental businesses with 1,890 active listings. Internal and test workspaces are excluded. Each call is placed in the local time of the property it's about, or of the business's main market when the call isn't linked to a listing; that matters for Hawaii, which runs 2 to 3 hours behind the West Coast. 11 calls with no known time zone are left out of the time-of-day figures, which therefore cover 6,785 calls. "Night" is 10pm to 6:59am, "evening" is 6pm to 9:59pm. Topics come from keyword matches on each call's AI summary, so a call can count toward more than one topic; we only report topics with at least 5 businesses behind them. The largest business accounts for 37% of calls, so we re-ran the key numbers without it: night share 4.5%, after-6pm access share 15.8%. The pattern holds.


## When the phone rings


Share of inbound calls to rental phone lines by local time, in three-hour bands


Local time at the property Share of calls


Midnight to 3am 1.3%


3am to 6am 0.8%


6am to 9am 7.0%


9am to noon 23.7%


Noon to 3pm 26.6%


3pm to 6pm 25.7%


6pm to 9pm 10.7%


9pm to midnight 4.1%


Calls track the hours guests are awake and moving: booking questions in the morning, arrival questions in the afternoon. After 9pm the line goes quiet, and between midnight and 6am it nearly stops. Across a typical business in this data, about **4% of calls come at night and about 15% after 6pm** .


That's good news for anyone who dreads the 2am call. It's rare. The catch is that the calls that do come at night are not a random sample of daytime calls.


## What callers want, by time of day


Topic in the call summary Day (7am to 6pm) Evening (6pm to 10pm) Night (10pm to 7am)


Booking, availability or price 24.6% 21.5% 22.1%


Getting in: door code, lock, keys, gate 8.7% 17.8% 16.5%


An existing reservation 10.0% 10.8% 12.5%


Something broken: plumbing, power, heat or AC, appliances 7.8% 10.3% 11.8%


Cancellation or refund 4.7% 3.1% 7.0%


Directions or the address 3.8% 3.1% 7.0%


Noise, parties or neighbors 1.4% 2.9% 3.3%


Three things stand out.


1. **Getting in is the night problem.** Late arrivals land after the host has gone quiet. The code didn't come through, the keypad battery died, the lockbox is stiff, the gate code changed. Once the sun goes down, access questions are about twice as common as during the day.
2. **"Can I book?" doesn't stop at night.** About a fifth of night calls are still about availability and price. Those callers don't need a person at 11pm. They need an answer and a link.
3. **Real emergencies are a small slice.** Broken things and noise together make up roughly 15% of night calls, and only a fraction of those can't wait until morning.


## Nobody picks up at night


**15.8%** of night calls never connected to anyone: no host, no teammate, no AI receptionist. During the day it's 12.5%, and in the evening 10.9%. A guest locked out at 11pm who gets voicemail usually tries again, then texts, then calls the platform. Each step makes the morning harder.


## Your after-hours call plan (copy this)


You don't need someone awake all night. You need a written plan for the few calls that come in. Copy this, fill in the blanks, and share it with whoever covers your phone.


**1. Answer without waking anyone**


- Door code or lock trouble when a backup exists: read out the backup code, the lockbox location or the spare key spot. Note it for the morning.
- Wi-Fi, TV, thermostat and appliance how-tos: answer from the house manual.
- Directions, parking and "which door?" questions: answer from the check-in instructions.
- Availability and price questions: give the dates and a link to book. Follow up in the morning.
- Cancellation and refund questions: explain the policy, promise a reply by ___ am, and log it.


**2. Wake the on-call person (name: ___, number: ___)**


- The guest can't get in and the backup didn't work.
- Water where it shouldn't be: a leak, an overflowing toilet, a burst pipe.
- No heat below ___ °F, or no power to the whole unit.
- Smoke, gas smell, carbon monoxide alarm, or any safety risk. Tell the guest to call 911 first.
- A noise complaint from a neighbor about one of your properties.


**3. Every night call, the next morning**


- Read the call summary.
- Fix the cause, not only the symptom: replace the keypad batteries, update the code in the check-in message, add the missing answer to the house manual.
- If the same question came up twice in a month, put the answer in the check-in message so nobody has to call.

## FAQ


### What percentage of vacation rental calls come at night?


In our data, 4.9% of inbound calls came between 10pm and 7am local time, and 17.3% came after 6pm. Across individual businesses the typical night share was about 4%.


### What do guests call about at night?


Mostly booking questions (22%), getting into the property (16.5%), questions about an existing reservation (12.5%) and something broken (11.8%). Access problems are about twice as common at night as during the day.


### Do I need someone on call overnight?


You need someone reachable for a short list of emergencies: a lockout with no working backup, water leaks, no heat or power, and safety alarms. Most night calls can be answered from your check-in instructions and house manual.


### How long are guest phone calls?


The median answered call in our data lasted 60 seconds. Most callers want one fact: a code, an address, a date.


### How do I stop lockout calls?


Give every property a backup way in (a second code or a lockbox), check keypad batteries at each turnover, and send the door code in the check-in message and again on arrival day. When a lockout call comes in, fix the cause the next morning.


## The takeaway


Night calls are rare, but they're the ones that hurt: a guest outside a locked door, water on the floor. Write down what gets answered and what wakes someone up, make sure every property has a backup way in, and make sure the phone gets answered when you're asleep.
